name: Uluwatu Temple
label: Uluwatu Temple
camera_source: Commons cluster (19 photos). Moved 17 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 20 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/707659668: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Uluwatu Temple' (111 m across).

text.description: Uluwatu Temple (Pura Luhur Uluwatu) is a Balinese Hindu sea temple on the south-western tip of the Bukit Peninsula. It sits right on the edge of a cliff about 70 metres high, with the sea below. That drop is why it photographs so well: the temple's dark stone and carved gateways sit against open sky and sea, and the cliff gives every frame a sense of height and distance. The temple is dedicated to Sang Hyang Widhi Wasa in his form as Rudra. It was greatly enlarged in the 11th century by the Javanese sage Empu Kuturan, and the name Luhur is linked to the later sage Nirartha, who is said to have attained moksha here. A Kecak dance based on the Ramayana is staged on the cliff-side in the evening, so there is a lot going on around sunset. Long-tailed macaques live around the temple and are known for grabbing cameras, sunglasses and flip-flops. Keep your phone in a hand or wrist strap and out of reach when you are not shooting. Take a wide view first to show the cliff and the sea, then move in on gateways, stonework and the edge of the headland. Check the official site before you go for access rules, any areas closed to visitors and performance details.
text.geographic_location: On the south-western tip of the Bukit Peninsula, in Pecatu village (South Kuta), Badung Regency, in southern Bali. The temple stands on a clifftop above the sea.
text.directions_text: Go by road from the nearest well-known town or area, such as Jimbaran or Kuta, by taxi, a ride-hailing app or a hired scooter, and head for the temple at the south-western tip of the Bukit Peninsula. Once you are there, find the phone icon on the map. The temple is 23 m to the south of it, about 1 minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the temple and cliff together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the sweep of coastline and sky, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out gateways and carvings from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the temple on one third of the frame, leaving the sea and sky for the other two. Keep the horizon level. With ultra-wide, keep the temple away from the edges so it does not stretch or lean. Include a path, wall or gateway in the foreground to give a sense of depth.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the temple stone to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. Near sunset, try night mode only if the light is really low, and hold the phone steady against a wall or your body. Keep a firm grip on it, because of the macaques.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into sunset suits the sea view, and the Kecak dance is staged at about 6pm. Check the official site before you go for current visiting arrangements.

text.access_note: This is a Hindu temple, so check the official site for visiting rules before you go.

name: Seminyak Beach
label: Seminyak Beach
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/17822273: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: 'seminyak' alone is the resort area; doubtful.

text.description:
Seminyak Beach is a beach in Seminyak, in Badung regency, Bali. It is the kind of place where the sky can do much of the work. With a horizon, a band of wet sand and waves rolling in, even a simple phone photo can have space and depth. The sand is a good surface for leading lines. Wave edges, footprints and the line where the tide has been all draw the eye towards the horizon.

The phone icon on the map is about 340 m north-west of the subject. From there the shoreline runs away from you towards the south-east, which suits a photo with a clear foreground, a middle stretch of beach and a distant horizon. If there are people on the beach, they can give a sense of scale and life when used carefully. If you would rather have an empty frame, wait a moment for people to move out of the shot.

Keep your phone away from spray and blown sand, and wipe the lens with a soft cloth before you start, as salty haze softens pictures. Stand on firmer, damp sand to keep your footing, and watch for incoming waves before you crouch down for a low angle. Take a few frames in a row as waves arrive, then pick the one where the water shape looks best.
text.geographic_location: Seminyak Beach is in Seminyak, Tibubeneng, Kuta, Badung, Bali.
text.directions_text: Travel by road from the Seminyak area, by taxi, a ride-hailing app or a hired scooter, and head for the beachfront near the phone icon on the map. Walk south-east along the shore or the beachfront until you reach it. The phone icon on the map is about 340 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full sweep of beach and sky, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out surfers, waves or distant figures on the sand.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 340 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Use it as a distant anchor and make the shoreline in front of you the main subject, or take the short walk towards it for a closer view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line, depending on whether the sky or the sand is more interesting. Let the edge of the wet sand lead the eye diagonally towards the south-east. Keep the horizon level, and add one person or object in the foreground for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sea or sky to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so bright sky keeps its colour and the sand does not wash out. Try a Live Photo or motion capture to catch waves, and pick the best frame afterwards. Use night mode only if the light fades after sunset, and brace your elbows against your body to keep the shot steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon towards sunset is often a rewarding time for softer, warmer light, though check where the sun sets from where you stand. Early morning is often quieter, if you want fewer people in the frame.

text.access_note: Beach access and rules can vary along the shore, so follow local signs.
claims_not_in_sources: Late afternoon and sunset light is often attractive here.
Early morning is usually quieter than late afternoon.

name: Mount Batur
label: Mount Batur
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/292801401: the OpenStreetMap point 'Mount Batur'.

text.description: Mount Batur is an active volcano on the island of Bali, northwest of Mount Agung, sitting inside a huge double caldera. The bowl-shaped caldera is about 10 by 13 km, and a 700-metre-tall cone rises from its floor above Lake Batur. That layering of rim, cone and lake is what makes it so rewarding on a phone. You can show the whole landscape in one frame, then pick out single details such as the cone, the water and the dark lava. The first recorded eruption was in 1804 and the most recent was in 2000. The large lava field from 1963 can still be seen from Kintamani, a town on the southwest ridge of the caldera, which is a good place to look across at the volcano. About 15 villages lie inside the caldera, including Kedisan, Songan, Trunyan and Toya Bungkah, so village roofs, fields and farmland can add foreground interest and a sense of scale. UNESCO added the caldera to its Global Geoparks Network in 2012. For photos, start wide to capture the shape of the caldera, then zoom in on the cone and the lava field. The phone icon on the map is at the volcano itself, so it suits a summit-area view. If you want the classic whole-mountain picture, step back to a ridge viewpoint such as Kintamani. Wipe your lens before you start, as haze and moisture can soften distant shots.
text.geographic_location: Mount Batur is in the Batur caldera on Bali, northwest of Mount Agung. Kintamani, a town on the caldera's southwest ridge, looks across to it, and the volcano is photographed at the spot itself.
text.directions_text: Go by road, starting from Kintamani, the well-known town on the southwest ridge of the caldera, and continue by taxi, a ride-hailing app or a hired scooter into the caldera. Villages such as Toya Bungkah and Songan lie inside the caldera if you want to be closer to the volcano. The phone icon on the map is at the volcano itself, so there is no walking distance or compass direction to give from it, and the route depends on where you start. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the caldera, lake and sky together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a natural view, then use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the cone and the dark lava field.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. This suits close-up views from the volcano. For a full view of the mountain and its lava field, move back to a ridge viewpoint such as Kintamani.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line. Include some foreground, such as a path, a wall, a field or the rim edge, to give depth. Keep the cone off-centre so the lake has room in the frame. Try a panorama to capture the sweep of the caldera, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the cone to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and detail. Use night mode only if the light is low, and hold the phone steady against a wall or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning often gives clearer air and softer light, but conditions vary, so check the weather on the day.

text.access_note: Access, any entry fees and trekking arrangements are not given in the sources, so check the official site before you go.

name: Ubud Monkey Forest
label: Monkey Forest
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9732447: large area 'Sacred Monkey Forest Sanctuary' (809 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
Ubud Monkey Forest, also called Mandala Suci Wenara Wana, is a sanctuary of about 10 hectares in the village of Padangtegal. It is a good place for phone photos because the monkeys, the old trees and the temple stonework all sit close together. As of 2023 around 1,260 Balinese long-tailed macaques lived here, and the grounds hold at least 115 species of tree. There are also three Hindu temples, all thought to date from around 1350. Mossy walls, shaded paths and monkeys grooming or carrying their young give you plenty of natural subjects without having to go far.

The monkeys are used to people and may come close. They are known to grab bags that hold food and to reach into bags and pockets, so keep your phone in your hand or a closed pocket between shots. Never offer food, and do not touch a monkey or pull food away from one, because that can provoke a bite. The better way to get a close picture is to stay at a distance and zoom in rather than step closer.

Some parts of the forest are not open to visitors. The sacred areas of the temples are for people who are there to pray and wear Balinese praying attire, so photograph the temples only from where visitors are allowed. Keep your phone's gridlines on and look for paths, steps and walls that lead the eye to a monkey or a carved gateway.
text.geographic_location: The forest is in the village of Padangtegal, in Ubud, Bali.
text.directions_text: Travel by road from central Ubud, the nearest well-known area, by taxi, a ride-hailing app or a hired scooter, and head for the Monkey Forest in Padangtegal. Walk slowly, as the paths can be busy with monkeys and other visitors. The phone icon on the map is about 160 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most shots of paths, walls and monkeys sitting nearby. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close-ups of faces and young monkeys, so you can stay well back. The ultra-wide (0.5x) suits the tall trees and the stone steps and gateways.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 160 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Take your pictures from the paths that visitors are allowed to use, and keep your distance from any monkey.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place a monkey or a temple gateway on a crossing point, with a path or wall leading towards it. Crouch a little for eye-level monkey shots, and keep your elbows tucked in and your phone firmly held. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) from a safe spot for the trees, and keep it away from people's faces.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the monkey's face to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so bright patches of light do not wash out the fur. Try portrait mode for a single animal against the greenery. Live Photos or motion capture help with a monkey that keeps moving.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day usually gives softer light under the trees and fewer people on the paths. Midday light can be patchy, so check the exposure slider if your shots look too bright or too dark.

text.access_note: This is a managed sanctuary where some areas are closed to the public and temple sacred areas are for worshippers only, so check the official site before you go for entry details.

name: Tanah Lot temple
label: Tanah Lot
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/6930069190: the OpenStreetMap point 'Tanah Lot Temple'.

text.description:
Tanah Lot is a temple on a large rock just off Bali's coast, and its name means "land in the sea". Pura Tanah Lot is an ancient Hindu pilgrimage temple, and it is one of the seven main Balinese sea temples along the island's south-western coast. It is dedicated to the sea god, and the 16th-century religious figure Dang Hyang Nirartha is also worshipped here. Visitors have long come to photograph it, and the reason is easy to see on the spot: a dark rock topped with temple roofs, waves breaking around its base, and open sea behind it.

A few facts help you understand what you are looking at. The rock can only be reached on foot at low tide. In the 1980s it began to crumble, and a Japanese-funded stabilisation programme followed. As a result, over one-third of the "rock" is now artificial rock made to blend in. A 2019 study put visitor numbers at around 500,000 a year, so expect company.

Keep the temple off-centre and leave space for the sea and sky. Watch the waves for a moment before you press the shutter, because a break of white water at the base adds energy. Wipe your lens first, as sea spray and humidity can leave a soft haze. Take a few shots at different zoom levels before the light changes, and then step aside so others can use the spot.
text.geographic_location: Tanah Lot is in Beraban, Kediri district, Tabanan Regency, on Bali's south-western coast. It is roughly 13 km south of Tabanan and 20 km north-west of Denpasar.
text.directions_text: Travel by road from Denpasar (about 20 km to the south-east) or from Tabanan (about 13 km to the north), by taxi, a ride-hailing app or a hired scooter. At the site, the path down to the sea runs between souvenir shops. The phone icon on the map is about 70 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the rock and the sea. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the cliffs, waves and sky all in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the temple roofs on top of the rock.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 70 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the rock on one of the vertical lines rather than in the middle. Leave a band of sea in front and some sky above. Keep the horizon level, and hold the phone steady with both hands, elbows tucked in.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the rock to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the rock stays dark but detailed. Try a Live Photo to catch the moving waves. In dim light after sunset, use night mode and brace yourself against a wall or rail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Low, warm light in late afternoon is generally flattering for the rock and the sea. When you face south from where you stand, the sunset direction will be off to your right.

text.access_note: This is a working Hindu temple on a tourist site: check the official site before you go for entry arrangements and any dress code, and note that the rock itself can only be reached on foot at low tide.
claims_not_in_sources: The sun sets in the west, which is to the right when facing south from the stand-here point.

name: Kelingking Beach (Nusa Penida)
label: Kelingking Beach
camera_source: Commons cluster (20 photos). Moved 16 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 110 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9869698: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: On Nusa Penida island: a boat trip from Bali.

text.description:
Kelingking Beach is on Nusa Penida, an island that is part of Klungkung regency, Bali. The photo is a sweeping coastal scene: a steep, rugged headland drops to the sea, with a small beach below and the ocean stretching out beyond. The scale is what makes it work. Cliff, sand and water fit into a single frame, and the colour contrast between green slopes, pale rock and blue sea reads clearly even on a small phone screen.

The phone icon on the map is the best place to start. From there the headland is about 106 m to the west, so you are looking along the cliff rather than straight down at it. Take a few shots from the marked point, then move a little along the viewing area to try different angles. Keep well back from the edge while you do. Cliff edges can be crumbly and the drops are big, so never step back without looking. Wear shoes with a good grip, and wipe your lens, because sea air and sunscreen smudge it easily.

This is a popular stop, so you may have to wait for a clear view. Be patient and polite, and take your shot when a gap opens.
text.geographic_location: On the south-western coast of Nusa Penida, an island in the Klungkung regency of Bali, at about 8.7513° S, 115.4731° E.
text.directions_text: You get to Kelingking Beach by road. From Nusa Penida's main towns, such as Toyapakeh or Sampalan, go by taxi, a ride-hailing app or a hired scooter. Once you are at the viewing area, find the phone icon on the map. The headland is about 106 m to the west of it, so you will be looking west to see it. The phone icon on the map is about 110 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic view of headland, beach and sea. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the coastline and sky in the frame. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the cliff shape or the waves on the beach below.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 110 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Stay behind any barriers and keep clear of the cliff edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the headland on one of the vertical lines, with the horizon on the top or bottom line. Leave some sea and sky around the cliff to show how big it is. If you include a person for scale, keep them well back from the edge and let them stand small in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the cliff to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and sea keep their colour. Try a Live Photo or a short burst when waves hit the beach, then pick the best frame. The panorama mode also works well along the clifftop if you pan slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people than midday. Check the weather before you go, because haze or cloud can flatten the view.

text.access_note: Access arrangements, any fees and safety rules at the viewpoint may change, so check the official site before you go.

name: Tegenungan Waterfall
label: Tegenungan Waterfall
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1454965010: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
Tegenungan Waterfall sits in the Saba area of Blahbatuh, in Gianyar regency. Waterfalls suit a phone camera well: moving white water against dark rock and green plants gives strong contrast, and you can get a good picture without any special settings.

Start with a wide view that shows the falls and the space around them, because this gives a sense of place. Then try a tighter shot of the water itself. People often add a figure to a waterfall picture to show its size, so you could ask a travelling companion to stand in a clear spot. Spray and damp air are common near waterfalls, so wipe the lens with a dry cloth before each shot. A smudged lens can make photos look soft or hazy.

Take a few frames rather than one, and check them on the screen before you move on. Paths and viewing areas near waterfalls can be wet and slippery, so watch your footing while you look at the screen. Access arrangements may change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Tegenungan Waterfall is in the Saba area of Blahbatuh district, in Gianyar regency, Bali.
text.directions_text: Go by road from Blahbatuh or the nearby Gianyar area, by taxi, ride-hailing app or hired scooter, and ask for Tegenungan Waterfall. The phone icon on the map is about 40 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full view of the falls. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the surroundings, and keep the phone level so the sides don't lean. Try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a closer shot of the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 40 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the falls on one of the vertical lines rather than dead centre. Include some rock or foliage in the foreground for depth. Take one wide shot and one tighter shot, and try both upright and sideways.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the falls to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white water keeps its detail. Try a Live Photo or motion mode to capture the flow of the water, and hold the phone steady with both hands. Wipe the lens first if there is spray.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go earlier in the day if you can, as it is usually calmer and the light is softer. In bright midday sun, the contrast between bright water and dark shade is harder for a phone to handle.

text.access_note: Access, entry arrangements and any fees are not confirmed here, so check the official site before you go.

text.description:
Kuta Beach is a beach in the Kuta area of Badung, Bali. It is a good place for relaxed holiday photos because beaches offer so much open space. You can include sand, surf and sky in one picture, and your phone can capture all of it without much effort.

Face that way and the shoreline should run away from you in a line, which gives a natural sense of depth. If people are walking, paddling or sitting on the sand, they can add scale and life to the picture, so wait a moment for someone to step into a gap rather than trying to clear the frame.

Beaches are often wide and bright, so the main challenge is usually light. Sand and sea reflect a lot of it, and a phone can make the scene look too pale or leave people too dark. Tap on the sand or on a person to set focus, then nudge the exposure slider down a little to keep the sky from washing out. Keep the horizon level by switching on the gridlines.

It is an open coastline, so conditions change with the tide, weather and time of day. Take a few frames as the waves come in and pick the best one afterwards. Wipe your lens before you start, because sea spray and sunscreen smear it easily.
text.geographic_location: Kuta Beach is in the Kuta area of Badung regency, Bali.
text.directions_text: Reach the Kuta area by road: take a taxi, a ride-hailing app or a hired scooter. Then head for the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is about 280 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the beach. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want the whole sweep of sand, surf and sky in one frame. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out a surfer, a figure on the sand or a distant stretch of shoreline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 280 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. You can walk towards it, about 5 minutes on foot, to get closer to the waterline.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line, not in the middle. Use the line of the shore as a guide leading into the picture. Hold the phone low for more foreground sand and a stronger sense of space. Wait for people to be spread out so that each one reads clearly.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sand or a person to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky and foam keep their detail. Try Live Photos or motion to catch the waves rolling in, and pick the best frame afterwards. In low light after sunset, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning and the hour before sunset usually give softer, more flattering light than midday, when the glare off the sand is strongest.

camera_source: Commons cluster (1 photos), weak. Moved 6 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 15 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.

text.description:
Ubud Palace, also known as Puri Saren Agung, is on Jalan Raya Ubud in Ubud, Gianyar, Bali. It makes a straightforward phone-photography stop, because you can frame the palace from a short distance away.

What works best here is keeping the frame simple. Show the palace with a little of its surroundings so visitors can see where it sits, and then move closer for details. Your phone's default colours should be enough, so there is no need for heavy editing.

If other people or vehicles are in the frame, wait for a gap rather than rushing the shot. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines of the building stay straight, and use the gridlines to help.

Check current opening and access information locally before you go, and respect any signs about where you can take photos.

name: Ulun Danu Bratan Temple
label: Ulun Danu Bratan
camera_source: Commons cluster (16 photos). Moved 47 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 60 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.

text.description:
Pura Ulun Danu Bratan stands on the shore of Lake Bratan in the mountains near Bedugul, and it is one of the most recognisable temple views in Bali. The shrines sit right at the water's edge, so the tall, layered thatched roofs sit beside the lake with the hills around it. That mix of water, roofs and hills is why it works so well on a phone.

The sources tell us the temple was built in 1633 and is used for offerings and ceremonies to Dewi Danu, the Balinese goddess of water, lakes and rivers. This is because the lake is a main source of irrigation in central Bali. The 11-storey pelinggih meru in the complex is dedicated to Shiva and his consort Parvathi. According to the source, when the Bratan River rises, the temple can look as if it is floating, which is why it is sometimes called the "Bali temple on the Lake". There is also a Buddhist stupa nearby, outside the main temple area, which stands for religious harmony.

Start with a wide view to show the shrines, water and hills together, then move in for details such as the roof tiers and the carved gateways. Keep people and bags out of the lower edge of the frame where you can. Remember this is a working place of worship, so keep a respectful distance from anyone praying and check the official site before you go for access details.
text.geographic_location: On the shore of Lake Bratan in the mountains near Bedugul, in the central highlands of Bali, at the middle of the 138-metre-wide temple outline (about -8.27548, 115.16646).
text.directions_text: Start from Bedugul and travel by road: take a taxi, a ride-hailing app or a hired scooter, and ask to be dropped at the temple entrance beside Lake Bratan. The phone icon on the map is about 60 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Begin with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the shrines on the water. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sky, lake and mountain, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the roof tiers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 60 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line. Include some water in the foreground and keep the temple roofs slightly off-centre. Zoom in on one roof for a tighter detail shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the temple to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright, so the roofs and sky keep their detail. Live Photos can catch ripples on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is usually calmer and more peaceful, and soft morning light can suit the scene; this is a general expectation rather than something confirmed by the sources. Check the weather first, as mountain cloud can come in quickly.

text.description:
Tegallalang Rice Terraces are stepped rice fields on a Bali hillside, and they suit a phone camera well. The terraces make curved, repeating lines that lead the eye through the picture, and the fresh greens give strong colour without any editing. Even a quick snap tends to look composed.

Stand there first and look in that direction. You can take a wide shot of the whole slope, then step closer and try tighter pictures of the curving rows.

For the wide view, use the default lens (1x) and turn on the gridlines. Line up one terrace edge with a grid line so the curves look deliberate rather than tilted. If you want to take in more of the slope, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Keep the phone level, because tilting it makes the terraces lean. For a more graphic picture, zoom to 2x or more and frame just a section of the pattern.

Paths and viewing areas can be busy, so wait a moment for a gap, or include a person in the frame to show the scale. Take your time and look around before you start shooting. Terrace edges can be uneven and slippery, so watch your footing and keep one hand free.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the terrace edges up with them so the curves lead into the picture. Keep the phone level and use the curving rows as leading lines. For depth, put a path, a palm or a person in the foreground.

name: Tirta Empul
label: Tirta Empul

text.description:
Tirta Empul is a Hindu Balinese water temple near the town of Tampaksiring. It is built around a holy spring, and Balinese Hindus come to the bathing pools for a ritual purification called Melukat. The temple was founded around the spring in 962 AD, in the Warmadewa dynasty, and the spring feeds the Pakerisan River. The compound has three courtyards: the front yard, the central yard and the inner yard. The central yard holds the pools and their row of spouts, and the temple is dedicated to Vishnu.

It photographs well because of the layers. Water, stone carving, temple gates and tropical trees all sit close together, and there is usually something happening in the pools. On a hill above the temple stands a villa built for President Sukarno's visit in 1954, a useful reminder of how long the place has mattered.

This is a working place of worship, so keep your phone shots respectful. Photograph the setting and the architecture rather than close-ups of people who are bathing or praying, and ask before pointing the camera at anyone. Keep your phone low and steady near the water, and wipe the lens first, as spray and humidity can leave it misty.
text.geographic_location: Tirta Empul is near the town of Tampaksiring, Bali, at about 8.4164° S, 115.3147° E. It sits beside the spring that feeds the Pakerisan River.
text.directions_text: Bali is best reached by road, so travel to Tampaksiring by taxi, ride-hailing app or hired scooter and ask for Pura Tirta Empul. From there, walk south-west for about 4 minutes on foot to reach the temple. The phone icon on the map is about 250 m north-east of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the pools and the line of spouts. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the wider courtyards to fit in gates and walls. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for carved details and water from a respectful distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 250 m north-east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the pool edge or temple wall up with a horizontal line. Use the stone gateways as natural frames. Include the water in the foreground and keep the carvings and trees behind it. Take a few shots with a person walking through who cannot be identified, to show scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the stonework and drag the exposure slider down a little so bright patches of sky and water do not blow out. Try a Live Photo of the flowing spouts, and choose the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer and the light softer, with fewer visitors. Later in the day the courtyards can be busy and contrasty.

text.description:
Tirta Gangga is a water garden in eastern Bali, built as a family retreat for the last king of Karangasem, I Gusti Bagus Jelantik, in 1946. It is named after the Ganges, the sacred river in India, and its pools are fed by springs on higher ground to the north-west. The Patirthan temple is part of the site, and the water has long been used as holy water in Balinese Hindu ceremonies. The whole complex covers about one hectare, so it is easy to cover on foot and you can try several angles in a short visit. The eruption of nearby Mount Agung in 1963 destroyed almost all of the complex.

It photographs well because water, stonework and greenery sit close together. That gives you reflections, repeating shapes and plenty of depth, even on a phone. Walk the edges of the pools before settling on a shot, because small changes in height and position change the reflections a lot. Keep people in the frame if you can, as they give a sense of scale. Wipe your lens before you start, since garden spray and humidity can smear it. Parts of the site may be ticketed or have rules for the temple area, so check the official site before you go.

text.description: Goa Gajah, the Elephant Cave, is a small cave sanctuary near Ubud, traditionally dated to the 9th century, though its style suggests the 11th century and its exact origins are uncertain. The cave mouth is surrounded by carved, fierce-looking faces, thought to keep evil spirits away, and that thick, textured stonework is the main reason it photographs so well. The complex mixes Hindu and Buddhist imagery. Inside are lingam and yoni symbols and an image of Ganesha, and by the river there are carved stupas. A bathing place with seven statues of women holding water pitchers was only uncovered in the 1950s, and the cave itself was rediscovered by Dutch archaeologists in 1923. The entrance is reached by walking down a long flight of steps, and the inside is small and often hazy with incense smoke. Expect to be on your feet on stairs, so keep one hand free for your phone. Shorts-wearers are given a sarong to tie on before entering the courtyard, which is part of the atmosphere. For photos, start at the phone icon on the map, where you can take in the whole carved entrance, then move closer for details. Stonework and moss look best when you keep the frame simple: one subject, such as the cave mouth or a single carved face. Please be considerate of people praying or making offerings, and avoid blocking the path. Check the official site before you go for current access details.

Pura Lempuyang Luhur sits high on Mount Lempuyang in Karangasem, east Bali. It is the seventh and highest temple of a complex of seven temples linked by a hiking path to the summit, at about 1,060 m above sea level. It is also one of Bali's nine directional temples, counted among the island's nine holiest places of worship, and is dedicated to Ida Betara Hyang Iswara, guardian of the east.

Most visitors come for the Penataran Agung Lempuyang compound, a separate temple in the complex. It has a tall white split gate (candi bentar), three dragon stairways and three kori agung gates, with views west towards Mount Agung, Bali's highest volcano. That combination gives a phone camera strong symmetry, clean white stonework and a big mountain backdrop framed by the gate.

For photos, work with the shape of the place. Within the gate compound, keep the gate square in the frame, let the stairs lead the eye upwards, and leave room for the volcano if the sky is clear. Cloud often gathers around mountains, so be ready to wait a few minutes or take a second look later. Because this is an active place of worship, be patient and respectful around people who are praying, and don't block steps or gateways for long. A dress code may apply, so check the official site before you go for current access arrangements.
text.geographic_location: On Mount Lempuyang in Karangasem district, east Bali, north of Amlapura, the regency capital. The map places the temple at the middle of the outline of Pura Lempuyang Luhur, which is about 72 m across.
text.directions_text: Come by road from the nearest well-known town, Amlapura, the regency capital. Take a taxi, a ride-hailing app or a hired scooter north from Amlapura to the slopes of Mount Lempuyang. The temples of the complex are linked by a hiking path up the mountain. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full scene, such as the gate, the dragon stairs and the sky together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, more natural view with less edge stretching. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out Mount Agung through the gap in the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The white gate and dragon stairs belong to the separate Penataran Agung compound. Here, simply find a spot with clear space around you inside or beside the temple area, and keep paths and entrances free for worshippers.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and, once you reach the gate, line the centre of the gate up with the middle vertical line. Hold the phone level and low to include the steps, and keep the frame free of people where you can, by waiting for a short gap. For portraits of friends, keep them off to one side so the gate still reads clearly.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the white doesn't burn out and the sky keeps its colour. Try portrait mode for people in front of the gate, and a Live Photo to catch a moment when mist moves through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier in the day is usually calmer and often clearer around the mountain, but cloud can come and go at any hour. Check the sky before you climb and allow a little spare time.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship on a mountain, so a dress code and entry rules may apply; check the official site before you go.

text.description:
Jatiluwih is a stretch of rice terraces in the Penebel area of Tabanan, Bali. The fields step down the hillside in curving lines, so the main appeal is pattern: rows of bright green or golden crops, narrow earth banks between them, and palms or small farm huts dotted about. A phone copes well with this kind of scene because there is plenty of detail and colour, and no single thing you have to get exactly right.

The phone icon on the map is at the same place as the subject, so there is no single direction to face. Turn slowly on the spot and compare the angles before you shoot. Look for a curve in the terrace edges that leads the eye into the picture, and try to include one small human-scale detail, such as a hut, a path or a tree, to give a sense of size.

The terraces are worked farmland, so keep to the paths, don't step onto the banks and give farmers room to work. Paths can be uneven or slippery after rain, so wear shoes with a grip. Bring a small cloth to wipe your lens, as humid air and a bit of dust can soften the pictures. Arrangements for entry or parking can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Jatiluwih is in the Penebel district of Tabanan regency, Bali. It is a farming area known for its rice terraces, and the spot is photographed from the terraces themselves.
text.directions_text: Bali has no railway-style public transport to this spot, so travel by road from the nearest well-known town or area, such as Tabanan, by taxi, a ride-hailing app or a hired scooter. Jatiluwih is in Penebel, Tabanan, so use Jatiluwih on the map to navigate. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the sweep of the terraces, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out patterns in distant terraces or a single hut.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Look around, choose the view that shows the most curving terrace lines, and shoot from there.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the top third, so most of the frame is filled with terraces. Use a curving terrace edge or path as a leading line, and include one small object, such as a hut or a tree, for scale. Try a panorama along the hillside if the terraces stretch wide.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the greenest area to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky doesn't wash out and the greens stay rich. Hold the phone steady with both hands, and wipe the lens first.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows across the terraces, and it is often more comfortable than midday heat.

text.access_note: Check the official site for access and any entry arrangements before you go.

text.description:
Handara Gate is a gate structure in the Pancasari area of Sukasada, in the Buleleng regency of Bali. It is a mapped photo spot, and a gate is easy to frame on a phone.

The gate suits simple, balanced pictures. Standing square-on and centring the gate gives a classic view. Stepping a little to one side gives a more relaxed angle that shows more depth. Vertical photos usually work well because they fit the full height of the gate and some sky.

The phone icon on the map sits right beside the gate itself, so you will probably need to step back to fit the whole gate into the frame. It may be busy at times, so be patient, wait for a clear moment, and keep the gate straight by using your phone's gridlines. Please keep to any rules on the day, and check the official site before you go to find out whether access is ticketed or restricted.
text.geographic_location: Handara Gate is in Pancasari, in the Sukasada district of Buleleng regency, Bali.
text.directions_text: Travel by road to the Pancasari area in Sukasada, Buleleng, by taxi, a ride-hailing app or a hired scooter. Head for Handara Gate for the final approach. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a straight-on view of the whole gate. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough to fit the whole gate in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close-ups of details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Step back a few paces from it, facing the gate, until the whole gate fits in the frame with some space around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the gridlines on and centre the gate, keeping the vertical lines straight. Hold the phone upright for a tall picture. For a different view, move a little to one side and let the edge of the gate lead into the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is bright, so the gate keeps its detail. Take a quick burst or a Live Photo while people move through, then pick the frame with the fewest strangers.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light. Mid-day sun can leave harsh shadows on the gate.

text.access_note: Access rules and any ticketing are not known, so check the official site before you go.
